articleContract.title: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software

story.title: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software

facts.text: The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write.
But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level.
AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff.

These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems.
Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code .
For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort.

After examining the data and AI usage telemetry of over 100,000 GitHub developers, researchers from MIT and UPenn’s Wharton School have determined that AI coding tools might help developers produce more lines of code, but that’s not leading to more finished software shipped.
IT Brew caught up with Greg Jennings, VP of engineering and AI at AI-native development company Anaconda, to understand what human bottlenecks stem from leveraging AI tools.
Brianna Monsanto is a reporter for IT Brew who covers news about cybersecurity, cloud computing, and strategic IT decisions made at different companies.
Similar disparities were observed when examining developers who relied on autocomplete tools, which suggest code as the developer types.
It is an argument that the adoption of AI coding tools without corresponding investment in codebase-level infrastructure is silently degrading the systems on which the global economy depends.
The engineers who maintain these systems are, in Adler's words, under siege from a flood of generated code they cannot fully understand or review.
Dan Adler, CEO of SourceCraft, told this story on the AI Engineer podcast, and it captures the collision he sees coming for every company running large, legacy software systems.
Adler's most technically specific argument concerns how large language models actually navigate code.
They "just love to search," he noted — comparing an agent to a new employee getting comfortable with a codebase — and this search behavior is how agents build their understanding.
Understanding requires context, and context at repository scale — 500, 5,000, 50,000, or half a million repositories — requires tooling that Adler says does not exist.
Agents are writing more code, faster, and he acknowledges their quality is improving.

The product iteratively implements changes across the codebase, independently fixes errors, responds to CI status and pull request comments, and uses code agents where judgment is required and deterministic scripts where consistency is required.
Adler's argument is counterintuitive: the AI tools that are making developers dramatically more productive are simultaneously undermining the stability of the codebases that run the world.
He calls it "a tsunami of code" — code being generated faster than enterprises can review, understand, or integrate it.

He rejects the obvious counterarguments — that agents can check code, that codebase-health tools exist, that model quality keeps improving — as "local maxima," dams built to contain a flow that keeps rising.
By his account, 72% of software industry workers are employed at companies with more than 500 employees — large global corporations managing thousands of repositories and decades of accumulated code.
Adler announced that Sourcegraph launched its new batch-changes agent into beta on the day of the talk.
The agent will search its way to understanding regardless of what documentation says.

The second unnamed quote Adler surfaces comes from a technical leader at a top-ten US bank, described as holding tens of trillions of dollars in assets in custody or under management: "Of course Claude Code can make this change, but I need to do it in 90,000 repositories." The context was a supply-chain vulnerability related to npm.

Adler ends with a diagnostic for codebase owners: how many repositories do you have, how many forks, how many copies, and how many repositories have your developers brought into the company that are now used as a library or API somewhere in production without your knowledge?

Well… The Wall Street Journal recently highlighted warnings from Mario Zechner and Armin Ronacher, two engineers behind core pieces of the popular OpenClaw AI agent, who argue that AI coding tools are flooding software with what they call “vibe slop.” Their complaint is that too many people are using AI to skip the parts of software development that actually matter: design, judgment, testing, ownership, and deep understanding of the system being changed.
You know, just describe what you want and let an AI coding agent build it.
This is why fleets of autonomous coding agents make me nervous.

As Honeycomb Founder and CTO Charity Majors puts it, being a great software engineer “has far more to do with your ability to understand, maintain, explain, and manage a large body of software in production over time, as well as the ability to translate business needs into technical implementation” than to simply churn out lots of code.
You cannot make tens of thousands of engineers, analysts, marketers, lawyers, and salespeople reliably “slow down and check the work” through good intentions and a memo.
In his talk, “The Friction Is Your Judgment,” he and Cristina Poncela argue that agent-generated code has a way of drifting toward the locally convenient answer.
In other words, AI doesn’t eliminate the need for engineering discipline.
That’s not as exciting as saying agents will write all your code but guess what?
